notes.source: 16 CFR part 318 (Health Breach Notification Rule), 2026 edition, § 318.2, "Breach of security", p. 1
notes.evidence: A breach of security includes an unauthorized acquisition of unsecured PHR identifiable health information in a personal health record that occurs as a result of a data breach or an unauthorized disclosure.

notes.front: Under the Health Breach Notification Rule, whom must a vendor of personal health records notify after a breach?
notes.back: Affected U.S. individuals, the FTC, and prominent media if 500 or more residents of a state are affected.
notes.explanation: The media duty is triggered by the number of residents of a single state or jurisdiction.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 318 (Health Breach Notification Rule), 2026 edition, § 318.3(a), p. 3
notes.evidence: (2) Notify the Federal Trade Commission; and (3) Notify prominent media outlets serving a State or jurisdiction, following the discovery of a breach of security, if the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of 500 or more residents

notes.front: Under the Health Breach Notification Rule, notices to individuals and media must be sent no later than {{c1::60 calendar days}} after discovery.
notes.back: 60 calendar days

notes.back: It may be logged and sent annually, no later than 60 calendar days after the end of the calendar year.
notes.explanation: Breaches of 500 or more must be reported to the FTC at the same time as the individual notices.

notes.back: B: the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule.
notes.choices:
A) The HIPAA Breach Notification Rule
B) The FTC Health Breach Notification Rule
C) COPPA
D) No rule: sharing is not a breach

notes.source: 16 CFR part 318 (Health Breach Notification Rule), 2026 edition, § 318.2, "Breach of security", p. 1

notes.back: A: within 60 calendar days after the end of that calendar year.

notes.front: Which 2016 law added the information blocking provision to the Public Health Service Act?
notes.back: The 21st Century Cures Act (Public Law 114-255).
notes.explanation: The section was added by section 4004 of that Act on 13 December 2016.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. § 300jj-52 (information blocking), source credit
notes.evidence: as added Pub. L. 114-255, div. A, title IV, §4004, Dec. 13, 2016

notes.front: What is the maximum civil monetary penalty for a health technology developer, exchange or network found to have committed information blocking?
notes.back: $1,000,000 per violation.
notes.explanation: The Inspector General investigates, and the penalty takes account of factors such as the nature and extent of the blocking and the harm.

notes.evidence: determined by the Secretary for all such violations identified through such investigation, which may not exceed $1,000,000 per violation

notes.front: A records software vendor deliberately builds its export feature in a nonstandard way so hospitals struggle to move patient data to rival systems. What is this most likely to be?
notes.back: C: information blocking.
notes.choices:
A) A HIPAA breach
B) A permitted business practice

notes.front: Which substance use disorder records does 42 U.S.C. 290dd-2 make confidential?
notes.back: Records of patient identity, diagnosis, prognosis or treatment kept by a federally conducted, regulated or assisted substance use disorder programme.
notes.explanation: Such records may be disclosed only for the purposes and in the circumstances the statute authorises.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. § 290dd-2 (confidentiality of substance use disorder records), § 290dd-2(a)
notes.evidence: Records of the identity, diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment of any patient which are maintained in connection with the performance of any program or activity relating to substance use disorder

notes.front: Without a court order or patient consent, may a Part 2 record be used in a criminal case against the patient?
notes.back: No: it may not be disclosed or used in civil, criminal, administrative or legislative proceedings against the patient.
notes.explanation: Such a record may not be entered into evidence in a criminal prosecution or civil action.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. § 290dd-2 (confidentiality of substance use disorder records), § 290dd-2(c)
notes.evidence: may not be disclosed or used in any civil, criminal, administrative, or legislative proceedings conducted by any Federal, State, or local authority, against a patient

notes.front: What form may a Part 2 written consent take, and what is its first required element?
notes.back: Paper or electronic; the first required element is the name of the patient.
notes.explanation: Other elements include who may disclose, a meaningful description of the information and the recipients.
notes.source: 42 CFR part 2 (substance use disorder patient records), 2025 edition, § 2.31(a)(1), p. 18
notes.evidence: A written consent to a use or disclosure under the regulations in this part may be paper or electronic and must include: (1) The name of the patient.

notes.front: Once a patient has consented, how may a HIPAA covered entity that receives Part 2 records use them for treatment, payment and operations?
notes.back: As the HIPAA regulations permit, and it may redisclose them in accordance with HIPAA.
notes.explanation: The statute ties post-consent handling for these purposes to the HIPAA rules.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. § 290dd-2 (confidentiality of substance use disorder records), § 290dd-2(b)(1)(B)
notes.evidence: Once prior written consent of the patient has been obtained, such contents may be used or disclosed by a covered entity, business associate, or a program subject to this section for purposes of treatment, payment, and health care operations as permitted by the HIPAA regulations.

notes.front: What must a Part 2 consent say about revocation?
notes.back: That the patient may revoke it in writing, except where the holder has already acted in reliance on it, and how to revoke.
notes.explanation: This is one of the required elements of a written consent.
notes.source: 42 CFR part 2 (substance use disorder patient records), 2025 edition, § 2.31(a)(6), p. 18
notes.evidence: The patient's right to revoke the consent in writing, except to the extent that the part 2 program or other lawful holder of patient identifying information that is permitted to make the disclosure has already acted in reliance on it

notes.front: A federally assisted addiction clinic wants to send treatment records to a patient's health plan for payment. The patient has signed nothing. What does Part 2 require?
notes.back: B: the patient's written consent before the disclosure.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, payment is always permitted
B) The patient's written consent before the disclosure
C) A court order
D) Only a notice of privacy practices
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is the HIPAA position, but the Part 2 statute requires prior written consent. C: a court order is not the route for routine payment. D: a notice is not consent.
notes.explanation: Part 2 records may be used or disclosed in accordance with the prior written consent of the patient.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. § 290dd-2 (confidentiality of substance use disorder records), § 290dd-2(b)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: Such contents may be used or disclosed in accordance with the prior written consent of the patient with respect to whom such record is maintained.

notes.front: How do the media-notice thresholds differ between the HIPAA breach rule and the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule?
notes.back: HIPAA: more than 500 residents of a state. FTC rule: 500 or more residents of a state.
notes.explanation: Exactly 500 residents triggers media notice under the FTC rule but not under HIPAA.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 318 (Health Breach Notification Rule), 2026 edition, § 318.3(a)(3), p. 3
notes.evidence: if the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of 500 or more residents of such State or jurisdiction is, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired during such breach

notes.front: How does HIPAA differ from Part 2 on disclosures for treatment, payment and health care operations?
notes.back: HIPAA permits them without authorisation; Part 2 requires the patient's prior written consent, though one consent can cover all future ones.
notes.explanation: Part 2 allows a single consent for all future such uses, easing the difference.
notes.source: 42 U.S.C. § 290dd-2 (confidentiality of substance use disorder records), § 290dd-2(b)(1)(C)
notes.evidence: It shall be permissible for a patient's prior written consent to be given once for all such future uses or disclosures

notes.front: After a HIPAA breach, how do the notice duties of a business associate differ from those of a covered entity?
notes.back: The business associate notifies the covered entity; the covered entity notifies individuals and, where required, the media and HHS.
notes.explanation: Both face the same 60-calendar-day outer limit.
notes.source: 45 CFR part 164 (HIPAA security, breach notification and privacy), 2025 edition, § 164.410(a)(1), p. 14
notes.evidence: A business associate shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected health information, notify the covered entity of such breach.
